extracted.intended_audience: proofreaders, copyholders, editors, authors, and typesetters (esp. University of Chicago Press editorial/printing staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and conventions for typography, composition, capitalization, italics, and related editorial/printing practices as used by the University of Chicago Press (early-20th-century Manual of Style). Intended to guide proofreaders, copyholders, and editors producing printed works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 1. Proper nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize proper nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns (e.g., George, America, North America, Englishman; Elizabethan, French).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize verbs derived from proper names (examples: to boycott, to fletcherize, to christianize, to pasteurize).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 2. Epithets used as substitutes for proper names or affixed to a name
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize epithets used as substitutes for proper names or affixed to a name (examples: the Pretender, Richard the Lion-hearted, Alexander the Great).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No additional exceptions noted beyond usage as substitute or affixed epithet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 3. Particles in French names when standing without a Christian name or title preceding
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize particles like 'le', 'la', 'de', 'du' when standing without a Christian name or title preceding (e.g., Le Bossu, La Torre, La Rochelle, De Coligny, D'Aubigne, Du Maurier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize those particles when preceded by a Christian name or title (examples: Ren^ le Bossu, Miguel de la Torre, Gaspard de Coligny, Thomas d'Aubigne, George du Maurier, Monsieur de la Torre, le comte de Nemours, le due d'Orl^ans). Always capitalize 'Van' in Dutch names; never capitalize 'von' in German names (examples: Stephen Van Rensselaer, Hugo von Martius, von Dobschiitz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 4. Generic terms forming a part of geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize generic terms that are part of geographical names (examples: Atlantic Ocean, Dead Sea, Baffin's Bay, Gulf of Mexico, Straits of Gibraltar, Mississippi River, Rocky Mountains, Mount of Olives, Prince Edward Island).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize such generic terms when they are merely descriptive additions to a specific name (examples: the river Elbe, the desert of Sahara, the island of Madagascar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 5. Adjectives and nouns used to distinguish definite regions or parts of the world
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize adjectives and nouns used singly or in conjunction to distinguish definite regions (examples: Old World, Western Hemisphere, North Pole, Equator, the North (= Scandinavia), the East (the Orient), the Far East, the Levant; the North, South, East, West (United States)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not as a rule capitalize adjectives derived from such names or nouns designating direction (examples: oriental customs, northern Europe, the southern states, a southerner). Exceptions noted (e.g., Northman = Scandinavian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 6. Generic terms for political divisions when part of names
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize political-division terms when they are organic parts of the name (Holy Roman Empire, German Empire, French Republic, United Kingdom, Cook County), when used with 'of' as integral part for certain administrative subdivisions (Department of the Lakes), when used singly as accepted designation for a specific division (the Union, the States), or when part of a fanciful/popular appellation used as if a real geographical name (Celestial Empire, Badger State).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize these generic terms when used alone or with 'of' preceding the specific name (examples: the empire, empire of Russia, state of Illinois).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 7. Numbered political divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize numbered political divisions (example: Eleventh Congressional District, First Ward, Second Precinct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No additional exceptions provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 8. Names of thoroughfares, parks, squares, blocks, buildings, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of thoroughfares and named places and buildings (examples: Drexel Avenue, Lincoln Park, Trafalgar Square, Monadnock Block, Lakeside Building, Capitol, White House).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic designations (courthouse, post-office, library) except when used with the place name or to avoid ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 9. Names of political parties, religious denominations, schools, and their adherents
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of parties, denominations, sects, philosophical/literary/artistic schools and their adherents (examples: Republican, Conservative, Christian, Protestantism, Catholic, Evangelical Lutheran, Epicurean, Stoic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize these words when used in their general sense describing spirit, trend, attitude, or mode of action (examples: republican form of government, socialism as an economic panacea, epicurean tastes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 10. Names of monastic orders and their members
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of monastic orders and their members (examples: Black Friars, Dominican, Jesuit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No additional exceptions noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 11. Proper (official) titles of organizations and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize official titles of organizations, institutions, and their names (examples: Union League Club, Smithsonian Institution, The Macmillan Company, Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize the generic term when used to designate a class or when standing alone (examples: young people's societies, the high school at Lemont, the club, the association), except to avoid ambiguity or where the word is consistently used as the name (e.g., He joined the Hall [Tammany]).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 12. Names of legislative, judiciary, and administrative bodies when specifically applied
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize specific names of bodies and departments (examples: Congress, Parliament, Supreme Court of the United States, Department of the Interior, Chicago City Council).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize general, paraphrastic, or incomplete designations (examples: the national assembly, the legislature of the state, the council, the department).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 13. Ordinals used to designate dynasties, sessions, regiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize ordinals used to designate such formally numbered entities (examples: the Eighteenth Dynasty, the Fifty-third Congress, the Second Illinois Regiment Band).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No additional exceptions provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 14. Commonly accepted appellations for historical epochs, language periods, geological ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names for epochs and periods (examples: Stone Age, Middle Ages, Renaissance, Reformation, Old English, Pleistocene).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No additional exceptions provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 15. Names for important events
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of important events (examples: Thirty Years' War, Revolutionary War, Louisiana Purchase).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No additional exceptions provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 16. Political alliances and historically significant secular/ecclesiastical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize political alliances and historically significant faction labels that function as parties or classes (examples: Protestant League, Holy Alliance, the Roses, the Roundheads).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where used in the general sense, capitalization may not be appropriate (see related rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 17. Conventions, congresses, expositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of conventions, congresses, expositions (examples: Council of Nicaea, Westminster Assembly, Chicago World's Fair).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No additional exceptions provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 18. Titles of specific treaties, acts, laws, bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles of specific treaties, juridical acts, and laws (examples: Treaty of Verdun, Declaration of Independence, Magna Carta, Fourteenth Amendment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Constitution (of the United States) is capitalized when standing alone; other constitutions are usually lowercased when referenced generically (e.g., the constitution of Illinois).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 19. Creeds and confessions of faith
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of creeds and confessions (examples: Apostles' Creed, Nicene Creed, Augsburg Confession, Thirty-nine Articles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also note on derived adjectives (lowercase: biblical, scriptural).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 20. Civic and ecclesiastical feast-days
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of civic and ecclesiastical feast-days (examples: Fourth of July, Labor Day, Thanksgiving Day, Easter, Passover, New Year's Day).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize 'sabbath' when used generically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 21. Titles preceding the name and academic degrees abbreviated following the name; titles of honor/nobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize titles preceding the name (Queen Victoria, Rear-Admiral Dewey) and academic degrees in abbreviated form following the name (Timothy Dwight, D.D., LL.D.); capitalize familiar or formal titles when used in place of the proper name and certain words like 'President', 'King', 'Pope' standing alone when referring to the existing incumbents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize titles when they follow the name (McKinley, president of the United States), when standing alone without the exceptions, or when followed by the name and preceded by 'the' (the emperor of Germany meaning not the existing emperor). See exceptions and examples in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 22. Abbreviated professional/political titles (Ph.D., M.P., F.R.G.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize abbreviations like Ph.D., M.P., F.R.G.S. and set them without spaces between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize the spelled-out phrase (doctor of philosophy, fellow of the Royal Geographical Society), except in special cases (see rule 25).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 23. One-letter abbreviations (except units and minor literary subdivisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize one-letter abbreviations such as R.V. (Revised Version), C. (centigrade), L.C.M., H.P., A.U., set without spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Units of measurement and minor literary subdivisions (see 54, 55, no, iii) are exceptions handled elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 24. Nouns and adjectives designating the Supreme Being or Power and pronouns referring to the same
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize nouns/adjectives referring to the Supreme Being (the Almighty, Providence, Father, Son, Holy Ghost) and pronouns referring to the same when not closely preceded/followed by a distinctive name or unless reference is otherwise clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize derived expressions like (God's) fatherhood, (Jesus') sonship, messiahship, messianic (but: Christology is capitalized). Examples and caveats provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 25. Words with acquired, limited, or special meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize words that have an acquired, limited, or special meaning (examples: the Doctor's degree; a report of the Master [in chancery]; a Bachelor's hood; a Freshman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize when the explanatory phrase renders capitalization unnecessary (examples: the doctorate, a master in chancery).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 26. 'Nature' and similar terms, and abstract ideas, when personified
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize personified terms and abstract ideas used as persons (examples: 'Nature wields her scepter mercilessly'; 'Vice' in moral plays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personification justifies capitalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 27. 'Father' used for church fathers and 'Reformers' for Reformation leaders when ambiguity would result
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the Fathers, the early Fathers, the Reformers when capitalization avoids ambiguity (examples: the Fathers, the Reformers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic descriptors like 'the church reformers of the fifteenth century' when context reduces ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 28. The word 'church' in properly cited titles of national bodies or when part of a named edifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Church' when it forms an inseparable part of a national body or edifice name (examples: Church of Rome, Church of England, Fifth Avenue Baptist Church).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize 'church' when standing alone or when the name is not correctly or fully quoted (examples: the church, the Roman Catholic church). Note: exceptional rhetorical capitalization allowed to emphasize antithesis between Church and State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 29. Names for the Bible and other sacred books
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names for sacred books and collective names (examples: Scriptures, Holy Writ, Word of God, Koran, Vedas, Apocrypha).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize adjectives derived from such nouns (biblical, scriptural, koranic, vedic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 30. Versions of the Bible
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize Bible versions (examples: King James's Version, Authorized Version, Revised Version, Septuagint).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use roman type for books of the Bible (see 31).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 31. Books and divisions of the Bible and other sacred books
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize canonical divisions and named books (examples: Old Testament, Pentateuch, Exodus, Psalms, Gospel of Luke, Acts of the Apostles, Epistle to the Romans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic words like 'book', 'gospel', 'epistle', 'psalm' when used generically (examples: the five books of Moses, the first forty psalms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 32. Biblical parables
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize named biblical parables when cited (example: the parable of the Prodigal Son).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No further exceptions noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 33. Miscellaneous biblical terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize certain miscellaneous biblical/religious terms with fixed significance (examples: Last Supper, Eucharist, the Passion, the Twelve, the Servant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow examples for usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 34. The first word of a sentence, and in poetry the first word of each line (English)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a sentence; in English poetry capitalize the first word of each line. In Greek and Latin poetry, capitalize only the first word of a paragraph, not each line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of English and classical usages provided; follow language-specific conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 35. The first word after a colon when it introduces a complete sentence or independent passage
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word after a colon only when it introduces a complete sentence or passage with independent meaning, or where the colon equals 'as follows' or 'namely'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize if the quotation/phrase is immediately connected with what precedes or if the colon introduces a brief explanatory phrase logically dependent on the preceding clause. Examples and exceptions provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 36. First word in enumerated sections when a link contains two or more distinct clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize first words in enumerations if an item contains two or more distinct clauses separated by semicolon/colon/period, unless all are dependent on same preceding term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate when to capitalize versus when to continue lower-case; see provided sample sentence with three enumerated reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 37. Nouns followed by a numeral indicating order in a sequence (esp. with Roman numerals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize nouns followed by a numeral that indicates sequence (examples: Room 16, Ps. 20, Grade IV, Act I, Vol. I, No. 2, Book II).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize minor subdivisions of publications (examples: sec. 4, scene i, art. iii, chap. 2(ii), p. 7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 38. First word of a cited speech or thought in direct discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a cited speech in direct discourse whether preceded by a colon or comma (examples: 'On leaving he remarked: 'Never shall I forget this day''. )
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also rule 131 for punctuation interplay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 39. First words in resolutions following 'Whereas' and 'Resolved'
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first words following 'Whereas' and 'Resolved' in resolutions (examples: Whereas, It has pleased God...; Resolved, That...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No further exceptions noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 40. The exclamations 'O' and 'Oh'
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the exclamations 'O' and 'Oh' at the start of quotations or exclamations (examples: 'O Lord!', 'Oh, that I were home again!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 117 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 41. All principal words in English titles of publications and divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize all principal words (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, adverbs, verbs, first and last words) in English titles of publications and divisions (examples: The Men Who Made the Nation; The American College — Its Past and Present).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Botanical Gazette uses different practice; librarians often capitalize only first words in bibliographies — such exceptions may be followed in narrow measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 42. Capitalization in foreign titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules differ by language: Latin — capitalize proper nouns and derived adjectives; French/Italian/Spanish/Scandinavian — capitalize proper nouns but not their derived adjectives; German/Danish — capitalize all nouns but not adjectives (except German adjectival forms derived from persons); Dutch — capitalize all nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide language-specific examples (e.g., De amicitia; Histoire de la littérature française; Geschichte des deutschen Feudalwesens).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 43. Definite article in newspaper and magazine titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, as a rule, treat the definite article as part of the title when mentioning newspapers and magazines (examples: the Chicago Tribune, the School Review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No additional exceptions given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 44. Titles of ancient manuscripts (MS, MSS)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize manuscript titles (examples: Codex Bemensis, Cod. Canonicianus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use roman type; abbreviations MS/MSS discussed elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 45. Nouns forming part of hyphenated compounds in titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles with main words capitalized, capitalize all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds (examples: 'Twentieth-Century Progress', 'The Economy of High-Speed Trains').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize hyphenated components that are not nouns (examples: Fifty-first Street, 'Lives of Well-known Authors').

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 46. Scientific names in botanical, geological, and zoological matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, and genera; in botanical/zoological matter, capitalize species names if derived from personal names or generic names; in geological/medical matter, species names are never capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: Vertebrata, Reptilia, Salix; Fdis leo, Cocos nucifera (but geological examples: Pterygomatopus schmidti). See rule 71 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 47. Names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes (examples: Kafir, Negro, Hottentot, Makassar, Buginese).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No additional guidance; use accepted names.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 48. Names of astronomical bodies (sun, earth, moon exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of solar-system bodies except common nouns 'sun', 'earth', 'moon', 'stars' (examples: the Milky Way, the Great Bear, Saturn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lowercase for generic references (sun, earth) except in contexts; follow astronomical convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize — 49. Divisions, departments, officers, courses of study of the University of Chicago in official work
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of University divisions, departments, officers, and courses in official administrative/curricular contexts (examples: the University, the School of Education, the Department of Anthropology, the Board of Trustees, the President).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not capitalize generic references (the division, the department, the faculty) unless context or convention requires. Examples of preferred printing (caps and small caps for date lines and addresses) given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Capitals and Small Capitals — 50. Names of town and state in date line and salutatory/signature in letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the names of town and state in the date line, the salutatory phrase at letter opening, and the signature and residence at the end of letters in capitals and small capitals with specific indentation and alignment conventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: Chicago, Ill., January 1, 1910; 'My dear Mr. Smith:' centered/address lines in caps and small caps; date in caps and lower case; detailed layout recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set IN Small Capitals — 51. 'Whereas' in resolutions and 'Note' in notes and 'Section' in constitutions/by-laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize 'Whereas' in resolutions; set 'Note' (in notes, not footnotes) followed by period and dash; capitalize 'Section' introducing paragraphs followed by a number in constitutions/by-laws with customary abbreviation practice (Section 1 then Sec. 2, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of formatting and sequence provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set IN Small Capitals — 52. A.M., P.M., B.C., A.D.
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M. and P.M. (ante/post meridiem) and B.C. and A.D. (before Christ/anno Domini) in small capitals without spaces between letters (examples: 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C., 1906 A.D.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are to be set without spaces; see related rules for degree and title abbreviations (see 22, 103, 106).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Small (lower-case) Initial Letter — 53. Common words originally proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case initial letters for common words originally proper names whose origin is obscured and for verbs derived from proper names (examples: utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, boycott, roman (type), italicize).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of sample words provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Small Initial Letter — 54. Minor literary subdivisions and their abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Lowercase minor subdivisions such as chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note and use abbreviations chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related rules 37, no, and 236 for cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Small Initial Letter — 55. Units of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use lower-case initials/abbreviations for common units of measurement (examples: h.=hour, min.=minute, sec.=second; lb.=pound; oz.=ounce; yd.=yard; ft.=foot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set abbreviations in standard short forms; see full list in text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Small Initial Letter — 56. Italic side-heads capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads, capitalize only the first word and proper names; set all other words in lower-case initial letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 172 and 280 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Small Initial Letter — 57. First word of a quotation immediately connected with preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not capitalize the first word of a quotation that is immediately connected with the preceding text through conjunction or otherwise, even if it begins a sentence in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustrations and exceptions in rules 35 and 131.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize — 58. Words or phrases to which emphasis is desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases used for emphasis or importance (examples: 'This was, however, not the case').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use italics sparingly for emphasis; examples given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize — 59. Foreign words/phrases not incorporated into English
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize foreign words and phrases inserted into English text that are not yet incorporated into English; also single sentences or brief passages in a foreign language too short for reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of foreign institutions or places commonly used in English (examples: Pierre Lagrange, Freiherr von Schwenau, the German Reichstag). Also do not italicize words of everyday occurrence that have been anglicized (examples: per cent, entree, cafe, resume, naive). A long list of examples of words usually roman vs. italic is provided in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize — 60. Titles of publications and periodicals
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize titles of publications: books, plays, essays, cycles of poems, single long poems printed separately, pamphlets, treatises, tracts, documents, and periodicals (examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer Night's Dream; the Independent; the Chicago Tribune).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books of the Bible and titles of ancient manuscripts should be set in roman type (see 31 and 44). Note on house style variations (e.g., Botanical Gazette uses italics in text but roman in footnotes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize — 61. (begins) Treatment of books of the Bible and related items
rubrics_metrics.description: Indication that books of the Bible both canonical and apocryphal and titles of ancient manuscripts should be set in roman type rather than italics; cross-reference to rule 31 and 44.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text begins discussion and notes but is truncated in this excerpt. Use roman for biblical book titles; see related rules above.
